title: Civil-Document Runners for Immigrant Families
one_liner: A vetted in-country network that retrieves, verifies and delivers birth, marriage, police and court records for consular and NVC cases, with chain-of-custody proof and no forged shortcuts.
customer: Immigration law firms and family-based petitioners (largely South Asian, Filipino, West African and Latin American communities) who pay $150-450 per document, plus rush fees and bundled certified translation and apostille.
problem: Applicants wait on USCIS, but the delays that lawyers dread most sit at the National Visa Center and consulate: 'documentarily qualified' rejections, requests for secondary evidence, and 221(g) refusals for a missing or irregular civil document. Every country issues records differently, and the State Department's reciprocity schedule is only a starting point. Families hire fixers or relatives, sometimes receive forged or improperly obtained records, and then face a permanent fraud bar (INA 212(a)(6)(C)). Lawyers keep private lists of trusted runners abroad. They cannot scale and are not available to families without counsel.
solution: A managed marketplace of vetted local partners (lawyers, licensed document agents, registry liaisons) in 8-10 high-volume corridors (India, Philippines, Mexico, Dominican Republic, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nigeria, Vietnam, El Salvador, Haiti). Each order starts with a pre-check against the consulate's actual document list, then a tracked retrieval from the issuing office with receipt and photo proof, an 'authenticity file' documenting exactly how the record was obtained, and delivery bundled with certified translation, apostille where applicable, and secondary-evidence packets when a record truly doesn't exist. Use online registries (India DigiLocker, Philippines PSA, Mexico's online actas) wherever possible so that most orders need little or no physical runner.
why_now: Consular processing has become slower and more discretionary, with more document-authenticity scrutiny, more public-charge-related evidence demands, and periodic pauses or holds by nationality. Errors that used to cost weeks now cost months. Many civil registries have digitized since 2020, so remote retrieval is now feasible for a meaningful share of documents, which makes a thin-margin logistics business viable for a small team.
revenue_model: Per-document fee ($150-450 depending on country and rush), roughly 40-50% gross margin after local partner costs, plus bundled translation and apostille, and a subscription tier for firms that order 20 or more documents a month.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody thinks of immigration as a logistics problem, so VCs fund form software while the real bottleneck is a birth certificate in a district registry that doesn't respond to email. The valuable asset is not software but a scorecard of which local partners and registry offices actually deliver on time and produce documents consulates accept. Reliability data by country and office can be built only by handling volume, and that is a moat lawyers already acknowledge privately.
first_30_days: Pick three corridors (Philippines, Mexico, India) where much of the retrieval can be done through official online portals plus one local partner. Sign 2 partners per corridor and pilot with 5 family-immigration firms at a flat price per document. Handle every order by hand, log time-to-delivery and rejection rates by office, and publish a country-by-country reliability guide to attract the next firms.

title: Loss-Curve Intelligence for Autonomous Trucking Insurance
one_liner: A benchmark and risk-scoring workbench that helps insurers, brokers and carriers price driverless-truck coverage using evidence instead of 'unknown'.
customer: Specialty insurers and reinsurers, MGAs, brokers, and large trucking carriers. AV operators such as Aurora, Kodiak, Bot Auto and Gatik also buy, to lower their premiums.
problem: Insurers price AV trucks 'slightly above' human drivers purely because of the unknown, with premiums expected to fall 15-25% a year. Werner's CIO says 'we have a gap' on pricing. Nobody has normalized exposure data by operating domain.
solution: Ingest public crash reports (NHTSA Standing General Order and state reports), published safety cases and operator-contributed telemetry. Build frequency and severity priors by operating design domain (lane type, speed, weather, time of day) and deliver a quarterly benchmark plus a route and lane risk-scoring API. Later, underwrite as an MGA.
why_now: Aurora exits 2026 with about 200 driverless trucks and 500k+ driverless miles, the first real exposure data, and targets 30,000 trucks by 2030. Insurers must reprice yearly and need evidence to justify each step down.
revenue_model: $75-250k a year in subscriptions from insurers and reinsurers, per-policy data fees, and MGA commission (10-15% of premium) once loss data supports it.
non_obvious_insight: The problem is not too few miles but the lack of a standard exposure unit. Whoever defines miles by operating domain as the accepted denominator becomes the FICO of autonomy, and operators will share data because it lowers their premiums.
first_30_days: Build an ODD-normalized frequency table from public NHTSA data. Interview 15 trucking and AV underwriters, send a free 'AV vs human benchmark' brief to 3 brokers, and close one $30k paid pilot with an MGA.

title: Vacant-Unit Meter Watchdog and Insurance Vacancy Log
one_liner: Uses utility smart-meter data that owners already have rights to, so PMs can catch squatters, leaks and freeze risk in empty units within hours, without installing any hardware.
customer: Property managers and owners of single-family and 2-to-20-unit portfolios (100 to 2,000 doors). They already pay the utilities on vacant units and carry standard dwelling or small-building policies with a vacancy clause. Buyer is the PM's ops director or the owner. Secondary buyers later are E&S and landlord-program insurers.
problem: When a unit is occupied, the tenant is the sensor and tells you about leaks. When it is vacant you are blind for 20 to 60 days. Water damage, squatters, stolen copper, AC left running and burst pipes all happen in that window. Most property policies restrict vandalism, water damage and theft after roughly 60 days of vacancy, and the claim gets denied or cut exactly when the loss is biggest. Squatter removal is also time-critical: in many states an intruder found on day 2 is a police trespass matter, while the same person on day 30 needs a months-long court eviction. Walk-throughs are weekly at best, and the maintenance tech skips them when busy.
solution: Vacancy Vitals connects to interval electric and water data through owner-authorized utility APIs (Green Button Connect, or aggregators like UtilityAPI). The owner's account is usually the one active during vacancy, so no tenant consent is needed. Rules fire on patterns: continuous 24/7 water flow (leak), electric baseline above the empty-unit norm (someone living there, a crypto miner, a grow), a heating or cooling setpoint far outside range (pipe-freeze or mold risk), and a sudden drop to zero in a unit that should be running HVAC. Alerts go by text to the on-call tech with a one-tap 'send someone' button. The product also generates a time-stamped weekly vacancy-inspection log (data check plus a tech photo check-in) formatted for carriers' vacancy-permit or inspection conditions. That log is what preserves coverage.
why_now: Anti-squatter laws were passed in a wave in 2024 and 2025 (for example Florida and Georgia), which makes early detection more valuable. Smart-meter penetration passed roughly 70% of US electric customers. Insurers have been tightening on water-damage and vacancy exposure for several years. AI-based anomaly detection on interval data is now cheap. (Current state-by-state anti-squatter rules and utility API coverage should be verified before launch.)
revenue_model: $4 to $7 per vacant-unit-month on usage, or a flat $1 to $2 per door per month portfolio subscription. Later, insurer-paid or insurer-discounted programs: the carrier pays a fee per monitored door in exchange for lower loss ratios and a vacancy-clause waiver.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest sensor for a vacant house is the meter the utility already installed, and the account is in the owner's name during vacancy. Nobody in proptech treats owner-account utility data as a security and insurance-compliance feed. They sell $60 leak sensors and cameras instead. The other secret is legal timing. The value is not detecting the squatter, it is detecting them in the first 48 hours, when the law treats it as trespass rather than a tenancy.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 to 5 SFR or small-multifamily PMs, offer a free 'backtest', and pull 12 months of interval data for units that were vacant. Show them the incidents the tool would have caught. These are usually a few leaks, a few unauthorized occupants and several HVAC-left-on units, each worth $1,000 to $15,000. Build a UtilityAPI-based prototype with three rules, text alerts and a weekly PDF log. Charge $99 per month per portfolio during the pilot, then convert to per-unit pricing. In parallel, talk to two independent insurance agents who write landlord programs, to learn the exact vacancy-permit language and to get a warm intro for the carrier channel.

title: FinOps for Open-Banking Data Spend
one_liner: Bank data access is turning into a metered cost. Do for aggregator bills what cloud FinOps did for AWS bills.
customer: Fintech lenders, budgeting apps and payroll and EWA apps spending $200k-$10M per year on aggregators (Plaid, MX, Finicity) and direct bank APIs.
problem: The CFPB 1033 rule is stayed, and a rewrite sent to OIRA on 2026-08-06 may let banks charge aggregators past a free-request threshold (PYMNTS). Developers over-poll accounts and pay per connection and per refresh, and a fee threshold would create sudden bill shock. Nobody owns the cost line.
solution: A proxy and observability layer that dedupes and caches pulls, replaces polling with webhooks and event-based refreshes, refreshes only when a decision needs fresh data (underwriting, payday), benchmarks vendor mix and price, and forecasts spend under proposed fee scenarios.
why_now: Regulatory uncertainty is at its peak, states like New York are proposing their own regimes, and fintechs face margin pressure. Any fee threshold in the rewrite turns data access into variable cost of goods sold.
revenue_model: 15-20% of verified savings (gainshare) or $2k-$10k per month SaaS.
non_obvious_insight: Data-access cost is becoming a real COGS line that finance teams can't yet see. My hypothesis is that dedupe and smarter refresh timing alone save 20-40%, so the first step is an audit that verifies it. A fee threshold makes that savings pool bigger.
first_30_days: Offer a free aggregator bill audit to 20 fintechs (they share invoices and usage exports). Quantify wasteful pulls, convert two to a 15% gainshare agreement, and publish the anonymized benchmark.

title: Neutral Noise-and-Flight Monitors for Drone Hubs
one_liner: Independent noise and flight-log monitoring that gives cities and neighbors a referee for drone-delivery hub permits, and gives operators and retail hosts approvable evidence.
customer: Drone-delivery operators and the retailers hosting hubs at store sites, paying to win and keep permits. City planning departments and neighborhood groups are the audience.
problem: Cities cannot regulate flight paths but can zone launch hubs. Northglenn requires a special-use permit, a 200 ft residential buffer and 65 dB at the property line. Wing and Walmart target 270+ sites by 2027 and Lowe's launched on Sep 28, 2026, so each site needs a hearing. Neighbors distrust operator-supplied noise data, cities lack staff and gear to check 65 dB, and a $5k-$15k consultant noise study is one-off and stale on day one.
solution: A permit-ready package. Before the application, a 7-day baseline at the property lines with calibrated low-cost acoustic sensors. After launch, continuous monitoring, tamper-evident logs, a public dashboard and alerts, matched to operator flight logs to attribute each event. An annual certification report cities can write into conditions of approval. Complaint triage: 'was a drone there at 3:14 pm? yes, 62 dB, within limit.'
why_now: The retail-scale rollout (Walmart/Wing 270+ sites, Lowe's/Wing/DoorDash launch on Sep 28, 2026, Zipline past 2M deliveries) is hitting local ground rules. Amazon paused after an Oct 2025 crane collision, so safety and trust are sensitive. Cities are drafting rules now.
revenue_model: $1,500 baseline and report per site. $300-$600/mo per site for monitoring, dashboard and certification. Optional city-charged permit fee. The city chooses the vendor, and raw data is public to protect neutrality.
non_obvious_insight: Local permitting, not the FAA, is the binding constraint on drone-delivery rollout. The currency of permits is neighbor trust, so a neutral measurement with a public dashboard is worth more than a better noise model. The party both sides accept as referee wins, and the fee is paid by whoever needs approval. Conflict-of-interest guards are the product: public raw data, no success fees, a firewall from operators.
first_30_days: Buy 10 sensors and calibrate them. Pick 3 cities with active hub hearings. Offer a free baseline for one live application at a store site. Get a city planner to reference the method in conditions of approval. Sign the first paid contract with a retail host or operator. Aim for 15-30 monitored sites by month 6.

title: Transfer-Portal Durability Passport for College Athletes
one_liner: An athlete-owned, verified injury and load history that programs will demand before they commit six figures of revenue share.
customer: College programs (general managers, sports medicine, compliance), collectives and agents pay for verified dossiers; athletes get their file free and own it.
problem: Chain: the House settlement lets schools pay athletes up to about $20.5M in 2025-26, unlimited transfers and the June 2026 shift to a five-year eligibility clock make multi-year, money-bearing roster bets, yet there is no standard electronic medical record across schools. Injury history moves by phone call and rumor: athletes fear disclosure, programs fear buying a torn ACL, and agents cannot prove durability.
solution: A consent-based portal where athletes' athletic trainers upload structured injury and return-to-play summaries, a standardized functional battery (jump/landing, isometric strength, hop tests) run at partner performance gyms, and optional load history exports from Catapult or WHOOP. The athlete chooses who sees what; the receiving program pays for a standardized, verified dossier.
why_now: Revenue-share contracts, unlimited transfers and the 2026 eligibility overhaul raise the financial stakes of injuries; the proposed Protect College Sports Act would add post-eligibility medical coverage duties and privacy protections; state privacy laws and HIPRA push consent-based data handling.
revenue_model: $150-300 per verified passport paid by the receiving program; $10-25k per year per program for scouting and post-signing baselines; $99 per athlete from agents.
non_obvious_insight: The athlete, not the school, must own the file: that is what makes disclosure acceptable and gives buyers something they can trust. It is a Carfax for players, and the customers now have real money at risk.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 mid-major and D2 basketball and volleyball athletes entering the portal through 3-4 friendly agents, build the consent form and one-page dossier, run 10 test sessions at a local performance gym, and pitch three assistant coaches or GMs on paying $200 per dossier.

title: Outsourced 24-Hour Vulnerability Reporting Desk (CRA)
one_liner: A retainer service that acts as the manufacturer's PSIRT: it watches for actively exploited vulnerabilities in their products' components and files the 24-hour early warning, follow-up notification and final report to the EU platform.
customer: Connected-device makers with 20-500 employees selling into the EU with no 24/7 security team: smart home, e-bikes and scooters, industrial sensors, routers, wearables, toys, EV chargers. Many are non-EU (US and Asian) firms.
problem: CRA reporting obligations began 11 Sep 2026: 24-hour reporting to ENISA for actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents, with fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. Small makers have no on-call rota, no SBOM monitoring and no idea what 'actively exploited' means for their firmware. The briefing found almost no visible tooling aimed at them.
solution: A retainer that ingests each product's SBOM per firmware version, matches it continuously against exploited-vulnerability and threat feeds, triages 24/7 with a pre-agreed decision tree, and files the early warning, notification and final report with text approved by the client's named contact. It also runs coordinated disclosure and advisory publishing, plus quarterly tabletop drills. Software lets one analyst cover 30+ clients.
why_now: The reporting duty went live 17 days ago and the full regime follows in Dec 2027. Firms are discovering that the deadline is a staffing problem, not a document problem.
revenue_model: EUR 1,500-6,000/month retainer, incident surcharges, and EUR 5k annual tabletop exercises.
non_obvious_insight: A 24-hour clock makes this a staffing obligation, which small firms cannot meet alone but a pooled desk can, like outsourced DPO services. Each reported vulnerability also gives a natural upsell into SBOM and technical-file work.
first_30_days: Partner with two or three EU security consultancies or product-safety associations. Sell a EUR 2.5k one-day 'CRA reporting readiness audit' to 20 firms, convert 5-8 into EUR 2k/month retainers, and contract three part-time analysts across time zones.

title: Large-Load Water Tariff Desk for Utilities
one_liner: An advisory-plus-software desk that gives small water and wastewater utilities the tariffs, effluent valuation and contract terms to negotiate with data centers.
customer: Municipal water and wastewater utilities and councils near data-center clusters (Texas, Arizona, Ohio, Georgia, Wyoming, Nebraska), plus investor-owned utilities preparing rate cases (the 15 largest private water companies invested about $6.8B in 2025). The utility pays.
problem: Step one: states restrict potable and groundwater for data centers. Step two: developers turn to treated effluent and offer take-or-pay deals under NDA. Step three: the small utility on the other side has no large-load rate class, no reclaimed-water price, no drought-curtailment priority and no analysis of downstream users who depend on its return flows. Electric utilities built large-load tariffs 12-24 months ago, and water is next.
solution: A 'Large-Load Water Tariff Toolkit': a cost-of-service model for a new large load, minimum-take and curtailment clauses, effluent valuation (including return-flow obligations), construction cost recovery, and reporting and audit clauses matching Texas and Australian rules. Entry product: a one-page 'your effluent is worth $X per acre-foot' for every discharge-permit plant within 30 miles of a data-center cluster, built from public discharge-monitoring data.
why_now: Texas froze ERCOT approvals on Aug 3, Ohio scrapped its general permit, and the Mississippi River states are drafting a compact. Regulators are asking who funds the extra infrastructure. Developers will sign deals in months, and the utility side has no playbook.
revenue_model: $30-150k fixed-fee engagements for tariff design and effluent valuation, SaaS for the cost-of-service model, and a success fee on an executed contract.
non_obvious_insight: The party with new bargaining power is the small wastewater utility, whose effluent just became an asset, but it is the least-staffed party in the room. Advising the weaker side of a deal is where the money is when the stronger side has all the lawyers.
first_30_days: Map all discharge-permit plants near known data-center campuses using public discharge and permit data. Produce 20 one-pagers. Email utility directors and city managers, and offer a free 45-minute briefing. Aim to close two paid engagements of $30-50k.

title: Surge Beds: Pre-Contracted Lodging for Catastrophe Responders
one_liner: Sell adjuster firms and storm contractors reserved-bed options on inland RV pads, seasonal parks and closed motels, contracted before landfall at prices that stay legal after an emergency declaration.
customer: Independent-adjuster firms' cat operations and logistics managers, restoration franchisees, roofing and mitigation contractors bringing out-of-state crews, and utility subcontractors. Reservation fees are paid pre-season, activation nights after the event.
problem: After landfall or a big wildfire, responder capacity is limited by beds, not people. Adjusters sleep in cars, 90 minutes away, or in RVs on borrowed lots, and deployed adjusters quit or rotate out. Anti-gouging laws (34 states, typically capping increases at about 10% for 30 days after a declaration) stop hotels from raising rates, so price cannot allocate scarce rooms; they simply sell out to whoever had a relationship or a corporate block.
solution: A lodging-capacity option network. Sign inland owners 60-150 miles from likely landfall zones (seasonal RV parks and park-model communities that sit empty in hurricane season, church halls and school gyms, closed-for-season motels, dorms, and short-term-rental owners willing to accept 30-day minimum stays) to pre-agreed rates that are lawful because they were set before the emergency. Buyers pay a per-bed or per-site reservation fee before the season, credited against activation nights. Add paid extras that responders actually need: Starlink, laundry, catering, portable showers, secure parking for trucks and trailers. Extend to wildfire base camps in CA, OR and CO.
why_now: Quick searches surfaced no dedicated adjuster-lodging option marketplace, only ad hoc use of RV parks after storms like Michael. Two years of quiet U.S. hurricane landfalls (none in 2025, and no hurricane at all in the 2026 Atlantic season through Sept 11) mean firms have not tested surge logistics and will be caught out by the next big one. Adjuster and contractor headcounts are being squeezed by automation and tight margins, so a predictable per-bed cost is more attractive than scrambling. Anti-gouging enforcement has grown more aggressive.
revenue_model: Reservation fees of roughly $400-$900 per bed per season, credited against activation nights. On activation, a 15-20% margin over the pre-agreed owner rate, plus ancillary services (connectivity, meals, laundry) at 30-40% margin. Later, annual enterprise contracts with IA firms for guaranteed headcount blocks.
non_obvious_insight: Because gouging laws freeze price after the declaration, the only legal way to buy certainty is to contract early, which turns lodging into an options market where the option seller (a snowbird RV park empty from June to October) has almost no other use for its inventory in exactly the months responders need it. Insiders know the constraint on a cat deployment is where 200 adjusters sleep, not how many exist.
first_30_days: Call 50 seasonal RV parks, campgrounds and small motel owners across the inland Gulf Coast, Carolinas and Texas and sign non-binding LOIs on rates and bed counts. Draft a one-page option contract reviewed by a hospitality lawyer for gouging-law compliance. Pitch logistics managers at 8 IA firms and restoration franchise groups on 2027 pre-season blocks, aiming for 2-3 signed reservation deposits of 20-50 beds each. Build a simple booking and check-in app with texted access codes and a map of inventory.

title: Tender-Time Snapshots: Post-Montgomery Broker Defense File
one_liner: A tamper-evident, per-load record of exactly what a broker knew about a carrier at the moment of tender, built to survive plaintiff discovery and to satisfy underwriters, then upgraded into a placed contingent-liability program for small brokers.
customer: Independent brokerages and host-agency networks doing roughly $2M-$60M in gross revenue that buy contingent auto liability through a wholesaler. Secondary payers: MGAs, wholesalers and E&S carriers that now need underwriting evidence.
problem: On May 14, 2026 the Supreme Court unanimously held in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II that negligent-hiring claims against brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA, so state-law suits now reach discovery. Insurance trade press (The Insurer, Sept 17, 2026, quoting RPS) is already calling it a capacity problem for broker contingent liability, and underwriters are asking for a paper trail of what was reviewed, when, and what was concluded. A small broker's carrier file is an onboarding PDF from 14 months ago plus email threads. Authority status, insurance, safety rating, ownership and contact info can change any day, and nobody can show what the screen said on the day of the load.
solution: Hook into tender events (TMS export, rate-con email forward, or load-board booking). At each tender, pull and hash-timestamp a snapshot: authority status, safety rating, insurance certificate validity, CSA/out-of-service rates, recent MCS-150 or contact-info changes, fraud flags, and which of the broker's own written selection rules the carrier passed. Any override is logged with a reason and the person who made it. A one-click 'selection file' export is formatted for a discovery request. Ship templates for a written carrier-selection standard drafted with trucking defense counsel. Phase 2: use the aggregated data to place small brokers into a wholesaler/MGA contingent-liability program with pricing credit for documented behavior.
why_now: Montgomery (May 14, 2026) removed the broad preemption defense. Contingent auto liability and E&O are repricing and capacity is tightening, per industry reporting in Sept 2026. The FMCSA broker financial-responsibility rule took full effect Jan 16, 2026, with suspension if security stays below $75K for 7 business days, so brokers cannot absorb a surprise verdict or claim.
revenue_model: SaaS at $0.50-$1.50 per tendered load or $300-$1,200/month by volume. Phase 2 adds a 10-15% commission on premium placed through the program, plus referral fees from defense firms.
non_obvious_insight: Plaintiffs' counsel does not ask 'did you vet the carrier?' They ask 'show me what your system showed at the minute you tendered, and who overrode it.' Brokers who vetted diligently at onboarding still lose, because they cannot prove tender-day state. Every broker knows the overrides happen at 4:45pm on a Friday when a load must be covered, and underwriters will price that override discipline. The record also proves the absence of red flags, which is the reasonable-care defense.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 small brokers through freight-broker Facebook groups and TIA chapters. Co-write a reasonable-care checklist with one trucking defense attorney. Build a snapshot logger on public FMCSA data plus an insurance-certificate check, ingesting tenders by CSV or forwarded rate-con emails so no TMS integration is needed. The sales hook is a free 'Discovery Fire Drill': simulate a plaintiff's request against the broker's last 5 loads and show the gaps. Convert at $299/month. In parallel, take the aggregate data to two wholesale brokers to test whether a premium credit is feasible.

title: Peak-Season Exchange for Idle Warehouse Robot Hours
one_liner: A marketplace and price index that moves idle AMRs and robots-as-a-service capacity between 3PLs and retailers to cover seasonal peaks, priced per robot-hour.
customer: Mid-size 3PLs and retailers needing Q4 peak capacity, and owners of idle fleets (integrators, RaaS providers, seasonal retailers, lenders holding repossessed units). Lenders and investors buy the index.
problem: Peaks force 3PLs into premium temp labor, while fleets sized for average load sit idle for half the year at seasonal operators. There is no market price for a robot-hour, so lenders cannot value the assets either.
solution: Standardize robot-hour listings (AMR class, payload, WMS integration) with a 48-hour commissioning kit (mapping, WMS connector) and escrowed insurance. Seed supply from idle demo pools and seasonal owners, and publish a weekly Robot Rate Index by class and region. Add forward contracts for peak later.
why_now: Robot pricing is becoming public and recurring (Figure's planned $600 a month lease, 1X at $499 a month, Agility's $300M+ order), and buyers want outcome pricing and 48-hour product-mix changes. Peak season 2026 is starting now, so the first rentals can be tested against real labor premiums.
revenue_model: 12-18% take rate on rentals, a commissioning fee per deployment, and $10-30k a year for index and benchmark subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Robots are sold as capex but bought as capacity. Once tens of thousands of units exist, capacity will trade like trailers and rail cars, and whoever runs the exchange sets the price benchmark (DAT, Drewry) and owns residual-value data.
first_30_days: Source about 50 idle AMRs from 2 integrators' demo pools and 2 seasonal retailers. Sell 3 emergency Q4 peak rentals to 3PLs paying temp-labor premiums, and publish Robot Rate Index v0 from about 40 collected quotes.

title: Together Suites: Adjacent Units for Grandparent Care
one_liner: Lease linked or adjacent apartment pairs to a young family and a grandparent, with a fire-rated interior door where code allows, a relocation concierge, and help getting the grandparent paid through child care subsidy relative-care rules.
customer: Multifamily operators with adjacent vacant units in lease-up (bundle premium or per-lease fee), families and relocating grandparents (concierge fee), and state child care subsidy programs paying eligible relatives.
problem: Informal care by relatives is the largest unmeasured slice of care and no property software or policy tool manages it. Two kids in center care cost more than rent in every state. CCDF already pays relatives (about 67,900 relative caregivers received payments in FY2023, 27.5% of CCDF providers), but few families know it, and grandparents live far away. Operators sit on adjacent vacant units and give free months to fill them.
solution: 'Together Suites': two separate leases, one bundle, adjacent units with an interior door retrofit (roughly $4-8K where fire ratings allow) or same-corridor pairs where they do not. A concierge handles the grandparent's move, health plan and licensing details, and where the state allows it and the family qualifies, enrolls the grandparent as a paid relative provider with the required background check and training. A shared schedule app and a backup nanny pool cover gaps.
why_now: Lease-up glut and record concessions make adjacent vacant units cheap to commit. A record share of house hunters (18.7% in Q2 2026) are relocating, often for family or price. Relative-care rules are established and under-used.
revenue_model: Operator pays $100-150 a month per suite, or a lease-up bounty per bundle, funded by lower concessions and better retention. One-time concierge fee of $500-1,500 to families. Optional payroll and background-check margin.
non_obvious_insight: Informal care is the majority of care but invisible to real estate. An owner's oversupply of adjacent units is the cheapest childcare 'center' ever built, staffed by people who will do it for love plus a subsidy, and two linked households with a shared schedule almost never move out.
first_30_days: Pilot in one lease-up building with four to six adjacent vacant pairs. File the door-retrofit permit. Advertise through grandparent-relocation Facebook groups, pediatric offices and local parent groups. Sign two bundles and track lease-up time, concession spend, and subsidy approvals. Start in states where relatives can be paid with light requirements.

title: Escaped-Burn Liability Cover Verified From Orbit
one_liner: Go/no-go data and liability cover for prescribed burn associations, priced from fuel dryness and settled by satellite proof that the fire never left the unit.
customer: Prescribed burn associations, contract burn bosses and private landowners (ranchers, forest owners) in Texas, Oklahoma, the Great Plains, the Southeast, Colorado and the West Coast. Surplus-lines MGAs, insurers and state forestry agencies are the second customer.
problem: Prescribed fire is the cheapest wildfire-adaptation tool, but escaped-fire liability cover is described as 'unavailable, unaffordable and vital' in places like Oregon and Colorado. Only a few risk pools exist, such as three Georgia burn associations with about 1,600 members. Insurers cannot price it because after an escape nobody has objective evidence of what was burned or when.
solution: Phase 1 is a software and certificate business that needs no insurance licence. A per-burn pack combines satellite live fuel-moisture and soil-dryness signals with forecasts as a documented go/no-go. A 72-hour containment certificate compares thermal hotspots (VIIRS, FireSat, commercial thermal) and next-day burn-scar perimeter (Sentinel-2 and Landsat at 10-30 m) against the permitted unit. Phase 2 has a partner MGA or risk retention group underwrite association pools, with verification making claims close to binary.
why_now: FireSat's first three operational satellites (July 2026) will deliver at least twice-daily data to early adopters by end-2026, heading to about 20 satellites and hourly revisit by 2029. Suppression backlogs and insurance retreat are pushing states to legalise more burning, and the Nov-Apr burn season starts within weeks. New free 10-30 m optical and radar archives make unit-level perimeter checks nearly free to produce.
revenue_model: $95-$250 per burn certificate plus $1.50-$3 per acre. Association memberships of $1-3K/yr. Later, MGA commission or a data licence to insurers underwriting pools.
non_obvious_insight: Prescribed fire is uninsurable not because it is risky but because nobody can prove afterwards that it stayed inside the line. An objective, cheap orbital perimeter check turns an unpriceable moral-hazard argument into an auditable event. Gross-negligence liability standards in state burn laws turn on documented preparation, which the go/no-go pack supplies.
first_30_days: Offer free winter-season pilots to 10 burn associations (TX, OK, NE, GA, CO) and build the containment check on free VIIRS, Sentinel-2 and Landsat data while applying for FireSat early-adopter access. Start charging $95 per certificate from December. Get one surplus-lines broker or MGA to review the certificate format as the seed of a Phase 2 pool.

title: Carrier Watchtower: Insurer Failure Alerts for Lenders
one_liner: Early-warning scores on the thinly capitalized insurers behind mortgage collateral, sold to servicers before the next carrier failure.
customer: Mortgage subservicers, credit unions, community banks and MSR investors with Florida, Louisiana, California and Texas collateral.
problem: Insiders treat Florida as fixed because Citizens fell from 936K to about 395K policies. But take-out carriers got Citizens' data to cherry-pick policies. A CBS investigation (unverified detail) alleges owners of a receiving carrier diverted millions. Howden warns reinsurer returns may fall below cost of capital by 2027, so any reversal hits the retail layer first. If a carrier fails, thousands of loans lose hazard cover at once and servicers must force-place at multiples.
solution: Loan tape in, exposure out. Map each loan's insurer from insurance-tracking data to a live stress score built from statutory filings, reinsurance program renewals, assumed-policy concentration, complaint ratios, rating actions and regulator orders. Give a 90-day warning and a pre-negotiated replacement placement lane.
why_now: Florida's rapid depopulation of Citizens in 2025-26 moved risk onto newer, thinner balance sheets. Reinsurance is at record capital and softening now, and the margin squeeze is forecast for 2027.
revenue_model: SaaS priced at basis points or cents per loan per year, plus per-policy replacement placement fees.
non_obvious_insight: Analysts watch carrier surplus and lenders watch loans, but nobody joins the two. Rating agencies lag, and the soft market hides the fragility.
first_30_days: Build dossiers on the top 40 Florida carriers from public regulator filings. Sell a $5K exposure report to two credit unions or subservicers showing what share of their book sits with the weakest carriers.

title: Service-Linked Loans for Vet Students Facing Caps
one_liner: Grad PLUS ended for new borrowers on July 1, 2026, and vet school now hits a $50K-per-year, $200K aggregate federal cap; clinics and rural practices can fill the gap with work-linked financing that doubles as retention.
customer: First- and second-year DVM students at high-cost programs (borrowers), and clinic groups, rural food-animal practices and state programs (employers who fund the retention hook).
problem: Veterinary medicine is one of 11 professional programs under the new caps, and out-of-state or private DVM costs can exceed $200K over four years, so students will lean on pricier private loans or cosigners. Meanwhile employers pay sign-on bonuses with no retention hook, and rural and food-animal practices cannot recruit; only 1.3% of vets are in food-animal practice, and South Texas is under strain from screwworm.
solution: A gap-financing product where employers pre-commit to fund a student's tuition gap in exchange for a 3-5 year service commitment with vesting forgiveness (like health-service scholarships). We underwrite, originate through a bank or CDFI partner, and administer vesting, recourse and state-incentive stacking, including Texas' funded rural veterinary incentive program.
why_now: The first cohort under the caps is enrolling this fall. Roll-ups are hungry for associates, Texas has funded rural vet incentives, and screwworm has made food-animal vet scarcity visible to policymakers.
revenue_model: 1-2% origination plus an annual administration fee paid by employers (8-12% of loan balance vested), and a spread on the loan book.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders see loan caps as a schools' problem. The second-order effect is that caps create a class of employers willing to pay to lock scarce DVMs four years early, turning tuition into the cheapest recruiting channel the industry has had.
first_30_days: Interview financial-aid officers at 4 high-cost schools. Sign term sheets with 3 employers (a rural practice group, a regional corporate group, a state program). Line up one bank or CDFI partner and get legal review on income-share and recourse rules in 3 states. Pilot with 10 students.

title: Off-Ramp Cohorts for AI-Companion Dependence
one_liner: Eight-week, in-person, non-shaming cohorts that help heavy AI-companion users rebuild human contact, sold to individuals and to employee assistance and counseling providers.
customer: Adults roughly 22-45 who spend two or more hours a day with AI companions (Replika, Character.AI, voice-mode chatbots), plus their worried partners and parents. Second wave: EAP vendors, university counseling centers and behavioral-health plans that have no protocol for this.
problem: Research suggests companions relieve loneliness in small doses but deepen it with heavy daily use; a two-year Aalto study of nearly 2,000 Replika users reportedly found heavy use raised the perceived cost of human relationships and tracked with more depression and loneliness. Lawsuits (Character.AI and Google settled the Garcia case in January 2026) and new laws (California SB 243 in effect since January 1, 2026, Washington HB 2225 signed in March) put the harm on the record, but clinicians have no playbook, users feel judged, and therapy waitlists are long.
solution: A harm-reduction curriculum, not abstinence. Week by week, participants audit what the companion provides (constant availability, validation, safe rehearsal), then re-home each need with a human equivalent: a weekly cohort dinner, a scheduled 'warm call' partner, rehearsal of hard conversations with a facilitator, and a graduated time-box on usage. Ten people per city per cohort, led by trained coaches with a licensed clinician supervising, screening for crisis, and referring out when needed. Pre/post measurement with a validated loneliness scale. Ends with a graduation dinner rather than a discharge.
why_now: Companion apps now have tens of millions of users, the APA flagged AI relationships as a major 2026 trend, and settlements and state laws have made 'what happens to heavy users' a public question. Operators under companion-chatbot laws need credible places to send users, and no incumbent exists. The EU AI Act provisions covering companion-style products are phasing in through 2026.
revenue_model: $395 per seat for an 8-week consumer cohort; $150-250 per seat through EAP and counseling partners; $1,200 curriculum license plus about $30 per participant for therapists and coaches who run their own cohorts; later, outcomes-based contracts with behavioral-health plans.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody pays to 'quit', but people pay to get more out of life, and the winning frame is nicotine-style harm reduction that meets the underlying need (low-stakes rehearsal, non-judgmental availability) with human structures. The competitor is not therapy, it is the AI, so the product has to be as easy to start as opening the app. Companion operators facing liability will eventually want a referral partner, which is a distribution channel nobody has built yet.
first_30_days: Recruit 12 participants from Replika, Character.AI and related communities with a screener asking who would try reducing use. Contract an LPC or clinical psychologist as supervising advisor and write a crisis-referral protocol. Run a 4-week pilot in one city in a cafe or coworking back room, charging $150. Collect pre/post loneliness scores and testimonials, then approach five EAP vendors and three university counseling centers with the data. Keep marketing to coaching and wellness, with no clinical claims.

title: Wearable-Verified PE Credit for ESA Families
one_liner: Turn any kid's fitness tracker into an audit-proof PE transcript line and an ESA service receipt.
customer: Homeschool and microschool families, co-ops and umbrella schools (about $10-15 per student per month). ESA administrators and clearinghouses (compliance contracts). Gyms and studios that want to bill ESA funds.
problem: PE is the least-supported homeschool subject. ESA homeschoolers get a fraction of what private-school kids do (about $2,000 versus $10,474 in Texas) and must spend in a closed vendor marketplace. ESA programs are audit-anxious. Local climbing gyms, swim schools and martial-arts studios cannot clear vendor onboarding. Screen-fatigued parents want real movement documented.
solution: An app plus a $40-60 band, or existing Garmin/Apple/Polar data shared with parent consent. It logs moderate-to-vigorous minutes and coach-attested skill milestones. It converts them into Carnegie-unit PE credit on a transcript issued through a partner accredited umbrella school. It also generates tamper-evident 'service delivered' receipts for ESA reimbursement. A vendor-of-record wrapper handles W-9, insurance and background-check attestations so a local gym can bill ESA funds. Parents control the data and only summaries leave the family account.
why_now: With 31 states opted into the 2027 federal scholarship credit and ESAs expanding, auditors and SGOs will demand evidence that services were actually delivered. Homeschool ESA marketplaces are closed and clunky. Alpha School has normalized heart-rate monitoring of kids, consumer wearables are ubiquitous, and 61% of teachers want less screen time.
revenue_model: $12 per student per month from families or co-ops. $2-5 per verified session or receipt from ESA clearinghouses. A 5-8% vendor-of-record fee on gym and studio ESA billings.
non_obvious_insight: As tens of billions of public scholarship dollars start to flow, the winning tools will be the ones that produce evidence of delivered service as a byproduct. A heart-rate trace is a hard-to-fake delivery receipt, and PE is the one subject where wearables give clean proof. Fitness providers' idle daytime hours are the supply, and education compliance is the demand.
first_30_days: In one ESA state (AZ or FL), recruit 8-10 homeschool co-ops and 3-5 climbing, martial-arts or swim studios. Sign an accredited umbrella school to issue the PE credit. Enroll about 100 kids for a semester at $12 a month. Ship a minimal web app that ingests Garmin/Apple Health exports plus coach attestation. Take the pilot data to one ESA clearinghouse.

title: Lake Ice Posts for Ice-Fishing Resorts
one_liner: Cheap solar LoRa thermistor-chain posts frozen into lake ice along access routes, giving resort operators and snowmobile clubs a live thickness trend and rate-of-change alerts on a seasonal subscription.
customer: Ice-fishing resorts and outfitters that rent ice houses and plow ice roads (Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, New York, Maine, Ontario), snowmobile clubs that groom lake trails, ice-derby and tournament organizers, lake associations and rescue units.
problem: Ice thickness varies across a lake and changes fast with warm rain, currents and springs. Resorts rely on daily manual auger checks at a few points. Vehicle and ice-house losses, and deaths, happen. Recent low-ice winters make timing harder. Research-grade buoys exist but cost far too much for a resort, and crowdsourced apps can't watch one specific corridor.
solution: A roughly USD 150 solar post with a thermistor chain spanning air, ice and water, plus a tilt sensor. It infers ice thickness from the 0 degree C interface and gradient, calibrated against the operator's own auger readings. Deploy 3-6 posts along the access road and ice-house village. The dashboard uses plain thresholds by vehicle class, texts an alert on rapid thinning, and offers an embeddable public 'ice conditions' widget for the resort's website.
why_now: It is late September, so units built now can be frozen in for this winter's first ice. LoRa, solar and thermistor chains are commodity. Ice-data apps (satellite radar, crowd reports) prove operators will pay for information, and research-grade buoys have validated the concept, leaving a low-cost tier open.
revenue_model: USD 199 hardware, plus USD 99-249 per post per season. Resort bundle of USD 1,500-4,000 per season. Sponsorship of the public widget by bait shops and outdoor brands. Contract work for counties and rescue units.
non_obvious_insight: Don't sell 'is the ice safe,' which is uncertifiable and a liability trap. Sell operational due diligence and a rate-of-change early warning: ice fails by trend (thermal decay, current), and a fixed post sees the trend before a weekly auger check does. Resorts lose money and reputation when they close roads early or lose a vehicle, so revenue protection is the wedge.
first_30_days: Build 25 posts before first freeze from off-the-shelf thermistor strings, LoRa boards and small solar panels. Sign 4-5 resorts to shoulder-season pilots at cost. Use their daily auger logs as ground truth. Launch a free public ice map to collect crowd calibration points and sponsors. Convert to season subscriptions and use winter data for next year's preorder round.

title: Turf-Ban Pivot Desk for Lawn and Irrigation Crews
one_liner: A done-for-you back office that turns lawn-maintenance crews into rebate-financed turf-removal and drip-conversion contractors, and uses their weekly routes as a cheap verification network for water utilities.
customer: Independent lawn-care, landscape-maintenance and irrigation companies with 5-40 crew members in drought-restricted Western and Texas metros. Secondary payers are water utilities and conservation funders.
problem: Their core product, mowing and irrigating turf, is being restricted and priced out as drought and utility rules spread. The replacement product (turf removal, drip conversion, native planting) is a project business with estimating, permits, rebate paperwork (pre-inspection photos, invoices, post-inspection) and financing, and national outfits are taking the work. Getting customers is small firms' #1 operational challenge in the Fed's 2026 survey, and legacy local-marketing vendors like Thryv are shrinking.
solution: A rebate-stacking engine per address (utility, county, state, supplier), net-cost-after-rebate estimates, photo-guided pre and post documentation, and submission with follow-up. Bridge financing against assigned rebates. Auto-generated local landing pages, Google Business Profile posts and mailers to the crew's existing maintenance clients ('your street qualifies for $X'). A route-verification add-on where crews photo-confirm turf has stayed removed so utilities can count the savings.
why_now: 49.6% of the US is in drought and the Colorado River 2027-2036 framework forces cuts. $7.2B of FY2026 SRF money is flowing. Corporate water-positive money, such as Amazon's $20M into the Water Resilience Coalition, increasingly needs verified savings that can be counted. Lower-cost LLM tooling makes per-address rebate rules and local pages cheap to produce for a 10-person crew.
revenue_model: 10% of rebate dollars processed (rebates on a job commonly run from several hundred to a few thousand dollars). 2% per month on bridge advances. $199/mo marketing add-on. $25-$60 per site per year from utilities or funders for route verification.
non_obvious_insight: The crew's client list and weekly route are the real assets. They are the only workforce already at every yard every week, which makes them both the best sales channel for turf conversion and a near-zero-cost inspection network to catch re-sodding, the thing utilities and funders need before they trust rebate savings. The subsidy is a sales script, not the product.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with a large turf rebate program. Find 5 lawn companies through the local green-industry association. Process 10 of their pending rebates free, then charge 10%. Publish a 'net cost after rebates' page for each crew's service area. Pitch one utility on a paid route-verification pilot covering 200 sites.

title: Resolution-Risk Ratings for Prediction Market Contracts
one_liner: A credit-rating-style score for how likely an event contract is to resolve ambiguously or be disputed, plus the rulebook basis between 'identical' contracts on different venues.
customer: Prop desks, market makers and arbitrage funds trading Kalshi, Polymarket and newer venues, at $300 to $3,000 per month. Venues and market creators pay for pre-listing rule linting.
problem: Polymarket logged more than 1,150 disputed markets in the first half of 2026, more than all of 2025. A US-Iran peace-deal market with over $345M in volume split traders on whether the outcome met a 'permanent' deal. Cross-venue arbitrage is not risk-free because sources, cutoffs and definitions differ, and displayed depth can vanish. Everyone prices the event, but nobody prices the contract wording.
solution: Parse each contract's rules (source of truth, timestamp cutoff, key definitions) and compare against a labeled history of disputes and oracle overrides. Output a 0-100 Resolution Risk Score with an expected haircut in cents. Give matched cross-venue pairs a scenario table of where they would settle differently, so arbitrageurs size positions correctly. Offer a 'rule linter' that flags ambiguous phrases for market creators, and deliver everything through an API and Discord/Telegram alerts.
why_now: Prediction-market volume is exploding (Kalshi reportedly passed $100B) and dispute counts are rising sharply. Institutional market makers are arriving and need risk inputs beyond price. Regulators and states are still fighting over these contracts, so rulebook and venue risk is priced by no one.
revenue_model: Desk subscriptions, per-market audit or lint fees from venues and market creators, and a data license to aggregators and terminals.
non_obvious_insight: Credit derivatives already lived through this. The asset's definition, meaning restructuring clauses and Determinations Committee rulings, became a priced factor, and an entire professional infrastructure grew around it. Prediction markets are at the 2003 CDS stage: the basis between 'identical' instruments is definitional risk. The winner is the rating-agency-plus-dispute-committee layer, not another odds aggregator.
first_30_days: Scrape resolved and disputed markets and hand-label about 300 disputes into an ambiguity taxonomy. Publish a public weekly 'Dispute Watch' with two or three calls that prove right. Sell to five arbitrage-bot shops through their Discord and Telegram communities at $500 per month. Offer free linting to prolific market creators for testimonials.

title: Router-and-Breaker Screen Control Sold by Trades
one_liner: HVAC, electrical and plumbing shops install tamper-proof, infrastructure-level screen and AI-companion controls as a maintenance-plan add-on for families with kids 8-15.
customer: Home-service shops with 5-30 techs and a maintenance-plan base (they resell the kit), and the parents of 8-15-year-olds who pay $199-349 to install plus $12-18 a month. Slow-season HVAC shops are the first wave.
problem: Under-16 social bans and school phone rules leak: VPNs cost under A$20 a month, seven in ten Australian under-16s reportedly still hold accounts, and only 29% of parents planned full compliance. App-level controls live on the device the kid controls, so they get uninstalled, and they cannot touch consoles, smart TVs, AI toys or AI companion sites. Parents want enforcement kids cannot delete. Meanwhile HVAC shipments fell 25-50% and shops have idle techs and a need for recurring revenue.
solution: A standard 'family network' kit installed in one visit, built from a hardwired or mesh router with router-level policies (VPN and proxy blocking, AI-companion and social categories by age tier, per-device schedules, guest SSID), plus smart-relay outlets ('kid circuits') for consoles and TVs, and a phone-parking charging nook. Parents manage it in a simple app, and shops get a two-hour training course and a quarterly tune-up visit. Cellular data is honestly disclosed as out of scope, and the kit aims at evenings and nights at home.
why_now: Bans and age-assurance rules are live in Australia, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Texas and Ohio, and Australia is proposing to double fines, so enforcement is the gap. The FTC's 2025 6(b) inquiry and state AI-companion laws put AI chatbots at the center of parental worry. HVAC is at a trough until a 2027 rebound, so shops want add-on services now.
revenue_model: Hardware-plus-install margin split with shops (about $75 spiff plus 30-40% of install), $12-18 per household per month recurring, and training and certification fees for shops.
non_obvious_insight: Software controls sit on the device kids control, so enforcement has to move to infrastructure parents physically own, and installing infrastructure is a trades skill. A local HVAC shop with 2,000 plan customers, most of them families, has near-zero customer acquisition cost compared with consumer parental-control apps.
first_30_days: Build the kit on off-the-shelf router hardware with DNS and VPN filtering and smart relays. Train two local electrical or HVAC shops and pilot 20 installs with a $75 spiff. Log bypass attempts and parent satisfaction, then sign five more shops using the pilot's numbers.

title: Alternative-Use Memos for Office Special Servicers
one_liner: A fixed-fee, five-day, non-conflicted resolution memo (convert, hold, sell, owner-user sale) for distressed office loans, written for the asset status report.
customer: CMBS special servicers, directing certificateholders (B-piece buyers), CRE CLO managers and bank special-assets groups handling office loans.
problem: About 15.7% of office CMBS is in special servicing, $39B matures within 12 months, and 71% of distressed balance is refinance failure rather than missed payments. Advice comes from brokers paid on transactions, and the standard resolution package (appraisal and broker opinion) rarely tests conversion, condo-ization or owner-user sale.
solution: An automated building screen (floor-plate depth, core, window line, structure, zoning, incentives, land-value floor) plus a local architect and contractor sanity check, delivered as a ranked options memo with recovery ranges, formatted for the asset status report. Public CMBS filings are used to prospect.
why_now: The 2026-2028 maturity wall is large and incentives for conversion are spreading. Vision and language models can screen buildings from public records, and servicers need defensible analysis for decisions that are now contested.
revenue_model: $6-12K per asset, sold in prepaid batches; retainers for servicers with 20+ office assets.
non_obvious_insight: The real buyer is the directing certificateholder who bears the loss and can direct disposition, and the cost is typically reimbursable from the loan and trivial against a $50M balance. A conflict-free second opinion can move recovery by points.
first_30_days: Use public CMBS filings to list 200 transferred office loans. Send a free sample memo on one publicly identifiable loan to asset managers at 10 mid-tier servicers and 5 directing holders. Price at $7.5K and target three paid pilots.

title: Second-opinion technical review for city data center deals
one_liner: A fixed-fee package for small cities facing a data center: adversarial review of the developer's noise, water and power submissions, plus a term sheet built from the few community benefit agreements that exist.
customer: Planning directors, city managers and county administrators in jurisdictions under a data center moratorium or first inquiry, mostly populations of 5k-150k that cannot afford a big-firm consultant. They pay $8k-25k per package, and the cost can often be recovered from the applicant through an escrow for third-party review.
problem: Small governments are negotiating blind against developers' consultants. Broken Arrow, OK issued an RFQ for consultants to 'advise on environmental, water, noise, utilities and fiscal modeling' and needs recommendations by year-end 2026 or a moratorium extension. Fort Worth voted unanimously for a moratorium, Chicago introduced one in September 2026, and Lexington, KY paused approvals until at least Oct 31, 2026. NPR reports that deals such as the one in Boyce, Louisiana were negotiated under NDAs. The Federation of American Scientists found only eight executed community benefit agreements, only one fully executed and publicly posted (Lancaster, PA), and says 'best practices are not readily available'.
solution: A productized package. (1) An ordinance with fill-in standards: setbacks, dBA limits at the property line, closed-loop or reclaimed-water requirements, decommissioning bond, and utility-capacity verification. (2) A fiscal calculator comparing abatement to service and infrastructure costs, plus water/wastewater and power-interconnection checks. (3) A term-sheet library annotated from the known executed CBAs. (4) A retained on-call review of the developer's noise study, water plan and load forecast by contract engineers, with a plain-language memo the council can read in open session. Moratorium end dates are natural deadlines that pull purchases forward.
why_now: Data center siting became the top local land-use fight of 2026: Wixom MI, Denver, Fort Worth, San Antonio, Lexington, Broken Arrow and Chicago all acted this year, and more cities keep opening moratorium clocks. Developer NDAs are now a political issue, which pushes officials to buy independent review.
revenue_model: $8k-25k fixed fee per package; $2.5k/month retainer during active negotiation; per-review fee for developer-funded escrow; a subscription comparables database (abatement terms, water allocations, decommissioning bonds) for state municipal leagues.
non_obvious_insight: Ordinance templates are free and cities can copy them; the scarce thing is an adversarial reader of the developer's technical submissions, because the city's only counterpart is the developer's own consultants under NDA. Applicant-funded escrow lets the city avoid a budget fight, so procurement is quick. Evidence: Broken Arrow's RFQ scope and year-end deadline (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9481196/oklahoma/tulsa-county/broken-arrow/city-council-meetings/city-forms-datacenter-study-committee-says-ordinance-moratorium-remains-in-place); the gap in best practices and only eight executed CBAs (https://fas.org/publication/data-center-community-benefit-agreements/); NDA-shrouded deals (https://www.npr.org/2026/08/27/nx-s1-5879528/data-center-nda-disclosure-louisiana); Fort Worth's unanimous moratorium (https://fortworthreport.org/2026/08/12/data-center-moratorium-takes-first-steps-after-fort-worth-city-councils-unanimous-vote/).
first_30_days: Publish a free comparison of the eight known CBAs and a one-page 'questions to ask a data center developer' for planning directors. Email 30 planning directors in cities with moratoria expiring in the next 6 months. Line up 2 retired utility or acoustic engineers as contract reviewers. Sell 2 fixed-fee review memos at $6k each, ideally funded by the applicant's escrow.

title: Diabetes Desk: Remote Glucose-Curve Review for Clinics
one_liner: CGMs and once-daily insulins made diabetic pets manageable at home, but nobody owns the workflow; sell clinics an outsourced desk that reads curves and proposes titrations for the DVM to approve.
customer: General-practice clinics with a dozen or more insulin-dependent dogs and cats. Secondary: pet insurers with diabetic cohorts.
problem: AAHA's 2026 guidelines split canine and feline diabetes for the first time and emphasize CGMs and once-daily insulins (degludec, glargine U-300). Owner burden is high and remote-monitoring services are thin. Clinics get a stream of curves they have neither the time nor a billing model to review, so pets stay poorly regulated. Tight control gives diabetic cats a real chance of remission, and avoids expensive ketoacidosis emergencies.
solution: Owners link a CGM to a clinic-branded portal. A desk of RVTs plus a consulting internist reviews curves weekly, flags hypoglycemia risk, and drafts dose-change suggestions for the clinic's own vet to approve within their VCPR. Includes SMS coaching on feeding and injection technique and refill/supply coordination. The clinic bills the owner a monthly program fee and pays us a wholesale share.
why_now: 2026 AAHA guidelines make CGM standard-of-care thinking. Long-acting insulins reduce injection burden. Ambient AI makes the record-keeping cheap, and remote-care rules are loosening piecemeal.
revenue_model: Clinic charges owners $59-99 per month; we take about $30-45 per patient per month. Later: outcome-based contracts with insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The clinical tech (CGMs, insulins, guidelines) arrived before the operating model. Human remote-monitoring took years to get billing codes; in vet medicine the owner pays directly and the value (fewer ER visits) is visible immediately, so a desk business can start without any payer.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 clinics and about 20 diabetic patients. Run a manual desk with one contract RVT and a part-time internist consult. Use CGM sharing links or screenshots to start. Track time-in-range and ER visits, and price the pilot at $79 per month.

title: Shopfloor Pulse: Voice-Agent Census of Job Shops
one_liner: Voice agents phone thousands of US machine shops monthly, publishing a real-time index of lead times, backlog and price pass-through.
customer: Macro and industrial hedge funds and alt-data desks, OEM sourcing chiefs and defense primes, PE and search funds hunting retiring owners, and regional economic developers.
problem: ISM surveys purchasing managers, not job shops, and MMS admits no dataset exists on shop ownership or retirement. Buyers cannot see real capacity or lead times, and funds rely on lagging government and PMI data despite July PMI at 55.6, prices at 71.1 and 12.64M jobs.
solution: Compliant, disclosed voice agents call about 3,000 shops a month with a four-minute script: quote lead time on a standard part, backlog weeks, materials surcharge, 5-axis or Swiss availability, and owner sale intentions. Combine with web and state-registry data. Publish a monthly index by region and process. Sell it as a subscription, and sell the resulting capacity directory to sourcing teams.
why_now: Voice models are cheap and natural in 2025-26, volatility makes non-consensus data valuable, and the retirement wave makes shop-level data valuable to buyers.
revenue_model: Alt-data subscriptions at $30-150k a year. Directory seats at $500-2k a month. Lead sales to search funds.
non_obvious_insight: The industrial base is tens of thousands of small firms nobody surveys, and the cost to survey them fell roughly 100x. A regional index that beats ISM by weeks is valuable because it is early, not because it is big. Telemarketing and TCPA rules need legal review, and calls should start human-assisted.
first_30_days: Build and legally review the script. Call 500 shops across three clusters. Publish a free preview index. Approach 10 alt-data desks. Aim for three paid pilots at $25-50k by month six.
